youtube.aciklama:
We explain the temporal bone that houses the ear: the pars squamosa, pars mastoidea, pars petrosa and pars tympanica, the mastoid air cells, the internal auditory canal, the key foramina and the course of the facial nerve through the bone. We also look at temporal bone fractures, mastoiditis and how the temporal bone differs in children.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Schuknecht, Pathology of the Ear.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will get to know the bone that houses the ear: the temporal bone.
We will see the four parts of the temporal bone, its key openings and its clinical importance for audiology.

notlar.metin: At the _side and base_ of the skull

cumleler: The temporal bone, os temporale in Latin, is a paired bone at the sides and base of the skull.
The inner part of the ear canal, the middle ear and the entire inner ear lie inside this bone.
In the section on screen you see the temporal bone and the hearing organ hidden inside it.
The facial nerve and the auditory nerve also pass through this bone.
The temporal bone borders the parietal, occipital, sphenoid and zygomatic bones, and forms a joint with the lower jaw.
Lying inside this hard bone protects the ear structures, but it also places them very close to one another.
So temporal bone anatomy is basic knowledge for both the audiologist and the ear surgeon.

ogeler.metin: Thin, flat plate at the temple
Bony wall of the ear canal

cumleler: The temporal bone is classically studied in four parts.
The pars squamosa, or squamous part, is the thin, flat part at the temple.
The pars mastoidea, or mastoid part, lies behind the ear and forms the mastoid process below.
The pars petrosa, or petrous part, is the hard, pyramid-shaped part that extends toward the skull base and holds the inner ear.
The pars tympanica, or tympanic part, is a curved plate of bone that forms most of the bony wall of the ear canal.
In addition, a thin, pointed projection extends downward: the processus styloideus, or styloid process.
Some of these parts are separate pieces at birth and fuse in the first year of life.

notlar.metin: Jaw joint: _in front of the ear canal_

cumleler: The pars squamosa is a thin, flat plate of bone to which the temporalis muscle attaches.
The zygomatic process extends forward and joins the cheekbone to form the zygomatic arch.
The mandibular fossa below this process receives the head of the lower jaw.
The jaw joint lies just in front of the ear canal, so jaw joint pain is sometimes felt as ear pain.
The pars tympanica forms the front and lower walls of the bony ear canal, and part of its back wall.
The edge of the tympanic membrane sits in a fine groove at the inner end of the bony canal; we will see this in detail later.
The pars mastoidea ends in the bony bump we can feel behind the ear, the mastoid process.
The sternocleidomastoid muscle on the side of the neck attaches to this process.
The inside of the mastoid is full of small, air-filled spaces that look like a honeycomb: the mastoid air cells.
These cells open into the middle ear through a large space called the mastoid antrum and a narrow passage called the aditus ad antrum.
So a middle ear infection can spread to the mastoid; this is called mastoiditis.
The development of the mastoid air cells is called pneumatization; it continues after birth and varies greatly between people.
This mastoid process is also where we place the vibrator in bone conduction testing.

sahneler.baslik: The petrous part: *home of the inner ear*

etiketler.metin: Inner ear inside the otic capsule

notlar.metin: Tegmen tympani: _roof of the middle ear_

cumleler: The pars petrosa is the hardest part of the temporal bone; its name comes from the Latin word for rock.
It is pyramid-shaped; its base is on the outside, and its apex points toward the middle of the skull base.
The inner ear, that is, the cochlea, the vestibule and the semicircular canals, lies deep in this hard bone.
The hardest layer of bone around the inner ear is called the otic capsule; it is among the densest bones in the body.
A bulge on the upper surface of the pyramid, the eminentia arcuata, marks the position of the superior semicircular canal below it.
Here a thin plate called the tegmen tympani forms the roof of the middle ear and separates it from the middle cranial fossa.
Because the tegmen is very thin, middle ear disease can, rarely, spread into the skull.
There is an opening on the back surface of the pyramid: the meatus acusticus internus, or internal auditory canal.
The facial nerve, the nerve for hearing and balance, and the labyrinthine artery that supplies the inner ear pass through this canal.
The far end of the canal is divided into upper and lower parts by a horizontal bony ridge.
In the upper part, the facial nerve lies in front and the superior vestibular nerve behind.
In the lower part, the cochlear nerve lies in front and the inferior vestibular nerve behind.
The vertical bony ridge that divides the upper part into front and back is called Bill's bar, after the surgeon who described it.
This layout explains why a mass in the internal auditory canal can affect hearing, balance and the facial muscles together.
The temporal bone has many openings and canals through which important structures pass.
The stylomastoid foramen is the opening between the styloid and mastoid processes; the facial nerve leaves the temporal bone here.
The carotid canal carries the internal carotid artery that supplies the brain, and it lies very close to the front wall of the middle ear.
Just below the floor of the middle ear lies the jugular bulb, the start of the jugular vein.
On the inner surface of the mastoid runs the sigmoid sinus, which drains blood from the brain.
Pulsatile tinnitus, heard in time with the heartbeat, can be linked to these nearby vessels; we will see this in later lessons.
The facial nerve follows a long, winding course inside the temporal bone.
It enters through the internal auditory canal and, after a short segment, makes a sharp turn at the geniculate ganglion.
It then runs inside the facial canal on the inner wall of the middle ear, just above the oval window.
Then it turns downward, descends through the mastoid and exits through the stylomastoid foramen.
Along the way, it gives a branch to the stapedius muscle and the chorda tympani branch, which carries taste fibers.
This long course through bone makes protecting the facial nerve very important in fractures and in ear surgery.
The temporal bone comes up in audiology in many clinical situations.
Temporal bone fractures can occur after head trauma.
Classically, longitudinal fractures are more common and mostly affect the middle ear, causing a conductive loss.
Transverse fractures affect the inner ear more often; sensorineural loss, vertigo and facial palsy can occur.
Today, fractures are also classed as otic capsule sparing or otic capsule violating; the latter has a more severe course.
Diseases such as acute mastoiditis and cholesteatoma also spread within the temporal bone.
Bone detail is examined with computed tomography, or CT, while nerves and soft tissue are examined with magnetic resonance imaging.
In infants, the temporal bone is clearly different from that of adults.
At birth, the mastoid process has not yet developed; it usually becomes prominent in the first two years of life.
So in infants, the point where the facial nerve leaves the bone is more superficial and more exposed to outside pressure.
The bony part of the ear canal is also absent at birth; the bony canal develops as the tympanic ring grows.
So an infant's ear canal is softer, and the pinna is pulled in a different direction for otoscopy; we will see this later.
The cochlea, however, is adult size at birth; the size of the inner ear does not change as the child grows.

sahneler.metin: After head trauma with hearing complaints, measure air and bone conduction together; the middle ear, inner ear or both may be affected. Share findings with the physician.
cumleler: A useful tip for the clinic: if a person with head trauma reports hearing problems, do not stop at air conduction testing.
In a temporal bone fracture, the middle ear, the inner ear or both can be affected.
Measuring air and bone conduction together shows the type of loss; ask about dizziness and facial weakness as well.
Findings are shared with the physician for referral; diagnosis and treatment decisions belong to the physician.

maddeler.metin: Mastoid cells open _into the middle ear_

cumleler: The temporal bone is studied in four parts: the pars squamosa, pars mastoidea, pars petrosa and pars tympanica.
The inner ear lies inside the hardest part, the pars petrosa, surrounded by the otic capsule.
The mastoid cells open into the middle ear through the antrum; infection can spread to the mastoid this way.
The facial nerve enters through the internal auditory canal, follows a long path through bone and exits through the stylomastoid foramen.

sahneler.soru: In which part of the temporal bone is the inner ear?
sahneler.aciklama: The inner ear is protected by the otic capsule inside the _pars petrosa_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in which part of the temporal bone does the inner ear lie?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: the pars petrosa, or petrous part.
The inner ear is protected inside a very hard bone called the otic capsule.
